title: Police shooting inquiry lacks focus on mental health system
subtitle: It is the elephant not in the room and it's a whopper, but where, at the Ontario coroner's inquest now probing the Toronto Police shooting deaths of three mentally ill people, is the provincial health ministry? The ministry didn't even bother to apply for standing - which gives parties the right to have a lawyer who can ask questions - and really, why would it have? This is not the broad inquiry into mental health that the deaths of three ill citizens truly demand.
article: It is the elephant not in the room and it's a whopper, but where, at the Ontario coroner's inquest now probing the Toronto Police shooting deaths of three mentally ill people, is the provincial health ministry? The ministry didn't even bother to apply for standing - which gives parties the right to have a lawyer who can ask questions - and really, why would it have? This is not the broad inquiry into mental health that the deaths of three ill citizens truly demand.

Lucky for all those hospitals, clinic directors, psychiatrists and psychologists, the inquest is focused on the tragic end to the lives of Reyal Jardine-Douglas, Sylvia Klibingaitis and Michael Eligon.
Thus the actions, inactions or failures of the various players involved along the way not only aren't being examined, the subjects aren't even up for discussion.

Only one hospital, Toronto East General, has standing at the inquest; it was from its quarters that one of the victims, 29-year-old Eligon, "eloped" after waiting 36 hours in vain for a bed, as the lingo has it.
Not much later, after a minicrime spree that saw him steal two pairs of scissors and arm himself, Eligon was shot by police.

Only one mental-health group, the Empowerment Council, has standing, and it's an advocacy group for clients (or "survivors," the preferred term) of mental-health services, primarily at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH). It is accountable only to its client members.

The inquest has heard now from more than 50 witnesses, and not one has testified about the de-institutionalization of Canadian mental health, its shattering effects and the fragmented mess that is the inarguable result.
As a Senate committee put it a few years ago, the mentalhealth care system is "not a real system."

And as the patient rights side of the equation has grown, so have services decreased, such that as the committee put it, people who won't accept voluntary treatment "are abandoned to the consequences of their untreated illness."
One of those, it appears, is that from time to time - Jardine-Douglas and Eligon, and Klibingaitis died in about an 18-month period - they will be shot by police.
And then there will be an inquest, like this one, which minutely studies police conduct without any reference at all to the factors that placed them in harm's way.
It is shocking, generally and in particular in the circumstances of the inquest.
Consider Tuesday's main witness.
She is Const. Shona Patterson, a remarkably capable young officer who at the time she encountered Eligon - it was about 10 in the morning of Feb. 3, 2012 - had six years on the job.

After he escaped Toronto East General, Eligon was acting so alarmingly that police began to receive 911 calls - from a woman he attempted to carjack, a storekeeper he stabbed in the hand with the scissors he stole, and someone else whose house he apparently broke into.

Patterson and her partner were in one of several squad cars that responded to the calls; she spotted Eligon, clad in a hospital gown, wearing black socks but no shoes, running across some backyards on Milverton Boulevard in the city's east end.

He was carrying the scissors the way you do, fingers laced in the holes, one pair per hand. She began shouting at him to drop them, to stop, and he looked right at her once, but without comprehension.
"One thing I remember," she said, "are his eyes. They were so brown and so big and so glossy, just nothing behind them."
From that first sighting until Eligon - who headed down a driveway to the street - was shot, she said, between 20 and 30 seconds elapsed.

In that half-minute or less, Eligon emerged onto the street, and the officers - there were about six of them by my count - began running and leaping backwards, as an in-car video from a parked police vehicle shows.

In fact, before the police or Eligon emerged on the video, a portion of which was played Tuesday, officers are heard yelling at him to drop the weapon and one is screaming to his colleagues, "Guys, back up! Back up!" And they did.
Eligon came into the picture, legs so thin under his gown. He walked stiffly, scissors in hand, deaf to the imprecations from the police.

"Did you think of trying anything other than yelling and screaming repeatedly?" asked David Landesman, one of the Empowerment Council lawyers, in his smirky way. He told a little story about a friend, with children, who purportedly told him that you can yell at them for misbehaving only so long. Then, according to this little tale, you try something else.
"I have no idea," Patterson replied.

Landesman then asked why she and the others didn't back up more. Did she wonder if "there was more that could have been done to ... create more space for him?" "I don't think so, at that point," she said.
"Do you think they could have moved faster?" Landesman asked.
"I think they did a great job," she said. "I think they did a great job."

She had her gun out; most of the officers with her did too. That's what they are trained to do when facing a person armed with an "edged weapon." In fact, police are trained to shoot when the person with the weapon is 21 feet from them; Eligon was within 10 feet of them when he was shot.
Patterson didn't fire, but she would have, she said.
When the gunshots came, and Eligon fell, Patterson raced to his side and did chest compressions. Then she helped the ambulance on its emergency run to a trauma hospital downtown.

How grating it is that the conduct of this exemplary officer, and her fellows, should be parsed so smarmily when the conduct of all those in the remnants of care that pass for a mental-health system - Eligon had been "treated" for his mental illness since 2003 - goes unexamined.
The inquest is all about the moment his troubles ended.
As someone smarter than me remarked recently, how much better, and fairer and more useful it would be to have begun at the beginning.
